--- title: "Method of Moments, MLE, and Bayes 🎯" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Point Estimation Techniques

Method of moments (MOM)

Likelihood and maximum likelihood (MLE)

Numerical MLE with `optim()`

Bayesian estimation and the bias-variance trade-off

::: notes - Two classical methods (moments, maximum likelihood) plus the Bayesian approach. Every derivation is followed by a numerical check. ::: ## Setting - A random sample $X_1, X_2,\dots,X_n$ carries information about the unknown $\theta$. - Observed values are $x_1,\dots,x_n$; in boldface $\bX$ and $\bx$. - The joint pdf (pmf) of an iid sample is $$ f(\bx\mid\theta) = f(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta) = f(x_1\mid\theta)\times\cdots\times f(x_n\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta). \qquad (1) $$ # Method of Moments ## Method of Moments Estimators - Equate population moments about the origin to the corresponding **sample moments**: $$ m_r = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^r,\qquad \alpha_r = \E[X^r] = \begin{cases}\sum_x x^r\P(X=x) & \text{discrete}\\ \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^rf(x)\,dx & \text{continuous}\end{cases} $$ - For $k$ parameters, solve the system $$ \begin{cases} \alpha_1(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k) = m_1\\ \alpha_2(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k) = m_2\\ \quad\vdots\\ \alpha_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k) = m_k \end{cases} $$ ## MOM Examples :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Bernoulli / Bin$(1,\pi)$:** $\alpha_1 = \pi \stackrel{\text{set}}{=} \bar X$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tilde\pi = \bar X$. **Bin$(n,\pi)$, $m$ samples:** $\alpha_1 = n\pi \stackrel{\text{set}}{=} \bar X$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tilde\pi = \bar X/n$. **Pois$(\lambda)$:** $\alpha_1 = \lambda \stackrel{\text{set}}{=}\bar X$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tilde\lambda = \bar X$. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **$N(\mu,\sigma^2)$:** $$ \begin{cases} \alpha_1 = \mu \stackrel{\text{set}}{=}\bar X = m_1\\ \alpha_2 = \sigma^2+\mu^2 \stackrel{\text{set}}{=} \frac1n\sum X_i^2 = m_2 \end{cases} $$ $\Rightarrow\ \tilde\mu = \bar X$, $\ \tilde\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum X_i^2 - \bar X^2 = S_u^2$. ::: :::: **Gamma$(r,\lambda)$:** $\E X = r/\lambda$, $\var X = r/\lambda^2$ $\Rightarrow$ $\tilde\lambda = \bar X/S_u^2$, $\tilde r = \bar X^2/S_u^2$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- rgamma(200, shape = 3, rate = 2) m1 <- mean(x); s2u <- mean(x^2) - m1^2 c(r_mom = m1^2 / s2u, lambda_mom = m1 / s2u) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r_mom lambda_mom 2.685 1.897 ``` ::: ::: # Maximum Likelihood ## Likelihood and Maximum Likelihood Estimators - Choose the value of $\theta$ that makes the observed data **most likely** under the model. - Once $\bx$ is observed, the **likelihood function** of $\theta$ is $$ L(\theta\mid\bx) = f(\bx\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta). \qquad (2) $$ - Same formula as (1), but (1) is a function of $\bx$ for fixed $\theta$; (2) is a function of $\theta$ for fixed $\bx$. (In the discrete case $L$ is no longer a probability.) - The maximizer $\hat\theta(\bx)$ is the **maximum likelihood estimate**; the statistic $\hat\theta(\bX)$ is the **MLE**. ## Log-Likelihood vs. Likelihood - Products are hard; the **log-likelihood** turns them into sums. $\log$ is increasing, so the maximizer is the same: $$ \frac{\partial \ln L(\theta\mid\bx)}{\partial\theta} = 0. \qquad (3) $$ - Products of many small densities **underflow** in floating point; sums of logs do not. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(2000, mean = 5) c(likelihood = prod(dnorm(x, 5)), loglik = sum(dnorm(x, 5, log = TRUE))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` likelihood loglik 0 -2806 ``` ::: ::: ## MLE Examples - **Poisson:** $\ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \sum x_i\log\lambda - \sum\log x_i!$, $\ \ell'(\lambda) = -n + \sum x_i/\lambda = 0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\hat\lambda = \bar x$. - **Exponential$(\lambda)$:** $\ell(\lambda) = n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum x_i$ $\Rightarrow$ $\hat\lambda = 1/\bar x$. - **Uniform$(0,\theta)$:** $L(\theta) = \theta^{-n}\,\mathbf 1\{\theta\ge x_{(n)}\}$ is decreasing on $[x_{(n)},\infty)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\hat\theta = x_{(n)}$ (calculus does not help here!). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1); u <- runif(10, 0, 3) th <- seq(2, 5, length = 400) plot(th, ifelse(th >= max(u), th^-10, 0), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#003366", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(L(theta)), main = "Uniform(0, theta) likelihood") abline(v = max(u), lty = 2, col = "red") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/05-estimation/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Likelihood and Log-Likelihood for a Normal Mean ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) n <- 10; mus <- seq(0, 10, length = 100); mu <- 5; x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu) Like <- function(mu, data = x) prod(dnorm(data, mean = mu)) logLike <- function(mu, data = x) sum(dnorm(data, mean = mu, log = TRUE)) max.L <- optim(1, Like, data = x, method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1)) max.logL <- optim(1, logLike, data = x, method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1)) L <- sapply(mus, Like); logL <- sapply(mus, logLike) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(mus, L, type = "l", lwd = 2); abline(v = max.L$par, col = 2, lwd = 2) plot(mus, logL, type = "l", lwd = 2); abline(v = max.logL$par, col = 2, lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/05-estimation/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(optim_L = max.L$par, optim_logL = max.logL$par, xbar = mean(x)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` optim_L optim_logL xbar 1.000 4.914 4.914 ``` ::: ::: ::: danger Maximizing $L$ directly fails here: at the starting value $L(1)\approx 10^{-35}$ is numerically flat, so `optim` never moves. Always maximize $\log L$. ::: ::: notes - fnscale = -1 turns optim into a maximizer. Brent's method (method = "Brent", with bounds) is a good choice for 1-d problems. ::: ## Numerical MLE: Gamma Distribution There is no closed form for the Gamma MLE of $r$. Maximize numerically, starting at the MOM estimate: $$ \ell(r,\lambda) = nr\log\lambda - n\log\Gamma(r) + (r-1)\sum\log x_i - \lambda\sum x_i $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- rgamma(200, shape = 3, rate = 2) nll <- function(th) -sum(dgamma(x, shape = th[1], rate = th[2], log = TRUE)) mom <- c(mean(x)^2 / var(x), mean(x) / var(x)) fit <- optim(mom, nll, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(1e-6, 1e-6), hessian = TRUE) rbind(MOM = mom, MLE = fit$par, SE = sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] MOM 2.6718 1.8875 MLE 2.7657 1.9539 SE 0.2616 0.2026 ``` ::: ::: - The inverse of the observed information (Hessian of $-\ell$) estimates the covariance of the MLE. ## MOM vs. MLE: Which Is Better? Simulate! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) est <- t(replicate(1000, { x <- rgamma(50, shape = 3, rate = 2) mom <- mean(x)^2 / var(x) mle <- optim(c(mom, mean(x) / var(x)), function(th) -sum(dgamma(x, th[1], th[2], log = TRUE)), method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(1e-6, 1e-6))$par[1] c(MOM = mom, MLE = mle) })) rbind(bias = colMeans(est) - 3, sd = apply(est, 2, sd), MSE = colMeans((est - 3)^2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MOM MLE bias 0.2003 0.1843 sd 0.7614 0.6529 MSE 0.6192 0.4598 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} boxplot(est, horizontal = TRUE, col = c("#FFCC00", "#88A0C8")); abline(v = 3, lty = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/05-estimation/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: # Bayesian Estimation ## Bayesian Methods - Information from the data $x$, a realization of $X\sim f(x\mid\theta)$, - is combined with prior information in a **prior distribution** $\pi(\theta)$, - and summarized in the **posterior distribution** (Bayes' theorem) $$ \pi(\theta\mid x) = \frac{f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)}{\int f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta} = \frac{f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)}{m(x)}, $$ where $m(x) = \int f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ is the **marginal density** of $X$. ## Example: Binomial Bayes Estimator - For $X\sim\text{Bin}(n,p)$, the conjugate prior is $\text{Beta}(a,b)$; posterior $\text{Beta}(a+x, b+n-x)$. - The classical Bayes estimator (posterior mean) is $$ \begin{aligned} \delta^\pi &= \frac{\Gamma(a+b+n)}{\Gamma(a+x)\Gamma(n-x+b)}\int_0^1 p\, p^{x+a-1}(1-p)^{n-x+b-1}\,dp\\ &= \frac{n}{a+b+n}\left(\frac xn\right) + \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\left(\frac{a}{a+b}\right). \end{aligned} $$ - A weighted average of the MLE $x/n$ and the prior mean $a/(a+b)$: a **biased** estimator of $p$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; x <- 14; a <- 2; b <- 2 post_mean_numeric <- integrate(function(p) p * dbeta(p, a + x, b + n - x), 0, 1)$value c(numeric = post_mean_numeric, formula = n / (a + b + n) * x / n + (a + b) / (a + b + n) * a / (a + b)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` numeric formula 0.6667 0.6667 ``` ::: ::: ## The Variance/Bias Trade-off - $\mse = \E(\delta^\pi - p)^2 = \text{Variance} + \text{Bias}^2$ measures average closeness to the parameter. - A small increase in bias can yield a large decrease in variance: $$ \var\delta^\pi = \left(\frac{n}{a+b+n}\right)^2\var\!\left(\frac xn\right) < \var\!\left(\frac xn\right). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- seq(0, 1, length = 200); n <- 20; a <- b <- 2; w <- n / (a + b + n) mse_mle <- p * (1 - p) / n mse_bayes <- w^2 * p * (1 - p) / n + ((1 - w) * (a / (a + b) - p))^2 matplot(p, cbind(mse_mle, mse_bayes), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c("black", "#C2185B"), ylab = "MSE", main = "MLE vs Bayes (Beta(2,2) prior), n = 20") legend("top", c("MLE x/n", "Bayes posterior mean"), col = c("black", "#C2185B"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/05-estimation/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: question For which values of $p$ does the Bayes estimator win? How does the picture change with $n = 200$? ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - **MOM:** match moments; simple, often a good starting value. - **MLE:** maximize $\log L$; invariant, asymptotically efficient; often needs numerical optimization (`optim`, Ch 14). - **Bayes:** posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior; posterior mean shrinks the MLE toward the prior mean. - Compare estimators by simulation: bias, SE, MSE. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
